newsitem.title: USA: Netcom seen unveiling new pricing.
newsitem.headline: Netcom seen unveiling new pricing.

text.p: Netcom Online Communication Services Inc is expected to unveil its new Internet access pricing scheme this week, a move that has been long overdue since its December announcement that it was scrapping its $19.95 a month pricing for unlimited service, analysts said.

In late December, Netcom, an Internet access provider in San Jose, Calif., said it would scrap its flat-rate $19.95 a month for a more profitable focus on the business market, leaving the consumer Internet access market to companies like America Online Inc, which has embraced all-you-can- eat pricing.

"They made this announcement several months ago and people have been wondering what is going on," said Marc Ussem, a Salomon Brothers analyst. "This company needs to bring some clarity to what the vision is."

Netcom is expected to unveil several product offerings and higher-priced flat-rate access packages, aimed at small and medium-sized business, offering faster access and premium customer support, analysts said.

One analyst who asked not to be named said that he expects a few different product offerings, in the $22 to $28 a month range. Netcom may also offer products for corporate intranets and for hosting corporate Web sites.
A spokeswoman for Netcom confirmed it plans to make its pricing and new product announcements this week, but she declined to provide any details.

Most analysts do not believe the company will begin any kind of metered pricing yet, because the company will risk losing many of its customers to other Internet access providers who are still offering unlimited Internet access for $19.95 a month. In February, Netcom said it had about 580,000 subscribers.

Since Internet access is becoming such a commodity, analysts said Netcom has to distinguish itself as a reliable, premium service for business users, who cannot have outages or busy signals that users were encountering earlier this year with America Online when it switched its users to unlimited access.

"It's a very important first step to hopefully what will be a good transition to addressing their small business market," Ussem said. "One reason the stock has been languishing is people are just waiting to see what they will do."
Shares of Netcom, like other Internet access providers, have dropped in recent weeks.
Netcom, which reached a high of $44 in May 1996, closed Friday at 8-5/8, down from about $15 in January.
